Pathology
The pathology of celiac disease was ﬁrst appreciated after the introduction of small intestinal capsule biopsy by Margot Shiner in
1956. The disease affects mainly the proximal small intestine, but the changes may be patchy. The pathology of jejunal capsule

biopsies was described in detail by Michael Marsh, who originated a classiﬁcation of histological severity (Oberhuber et al., 1999).
Currently the histology is evaluated on mucosal biopsies taken from the duodenum or jejunum during ﬁberoptic endoscopy of the
upper gastrointestinal tract. The Marsh classiﬁcation, as modiﬁed by Oberhuber, remains widely used in the reporting of duodenal
mucosal biopsies from patients with celiac disease (Table 1). In brief, the presence villous atrophy as well as crypt elongation or
hypertrophy, along with increased intraepithelial cells, remains the cornerstone of diagnosis. Type 1 and type 2 in the Marsh clas-
siﬁcation are not considered compatible with the diagnosis of untreated celiac disease, but may occur in patients on gluten free diet.
The Type 2 Marsh change may be seen in dermatitis herpetiformis. Complete villous atrophy (Fig. 1), seen in some patients with
celiac disease, is seldom if never not found in other small bowel mucosal diseases.
Clinical features
